wu: Students play 'Two Truths and a Lie' about Eid traditions. They write three statements on a card, two true and one false, then read them aloud. The class guesses which is the lie.
wuAlt: Students complete a 'Find Someone Who...' grid with Eid activities like 'Find someone who wore new clothes for Eid'.
Students draw a quick picture of their favorite Eid memory and share it with a partner.
pres: Show flashcards of Eid scenes (family dinner, giving gifts, visiting relatives). Model interaction phrases like 'I agree because...' and 'Can I add something?'. Check understanding by asking students to repeat the phrases in context.
presAlt: Read a short dialogue between two friends planning Eid celebrations. Highlight the interaction language on the board.
Play a recording of a PET-style Part 3 discussion about holidays. Students note down phrases used to agree and take turns.
prac: Students work in pairs with 'Eid Discussion Cards' with roles like 'You love the food' and 'You miss the gifts'. They practice using the interaction language while discussing the prompts. I circulate to offer support.
pracAlt: Students play 'Role Card Relay' where they draw a role card and must use the target phrase before passing the card to their partner.
Students complete a gap-fill worksheet with interaction phrases from the model dialogue.
ls: Students listen to a PET Part 3 recording of two people discussing Eid traditions. They complete a chart noting phrases used to agree, disagree, and take turns. We check answers as a class.
re: Students play 'Pass the Phrase' in a circle. I say an interaction phrase like 'That's a good point', and students pass it around the circle, adding a new word each time to make a longer sentence.
prod: Students form groups of three for a 'Family Eid Council' discussion. They use a rubric to evaluate each other's turn-taking and use of interaction language. Groups discuss 'How to make Eid more special for the family' and then retry the discussion with improved strategies.
rw: Students read a short article about Eid traditions around the world. They then write five discussion prompts for a PET Part 3 task, using phrases like 'What about you?' and 'How do you feel about that?'
st: I tell a personal story about my best Eid memory using the past simple and continuous. We end with the goodbye routine: 'Today we practiced taking turns in discussions. Thank you for your participation.'
g: Students stand in a line. I read a statement like 'Eid gifts are the best part'. They move to the left if they agree, right if they disagree, and say why.
Students sit in a circle. They toss a soft ball and must speak until they catch it again, practicing equal turn length.
Teams race to write interaction phrases on the board from memory after seeing them for 30 seconds.
Students swap role cards mid-discussion to practice adapting to new perspectives.
Students write their ideas on a shared paper, using symbols like '?' to ask for turn, drawing out the interaction silently.
diff: Fast finishers: Write a dialogue between two friends planning a surprise Eid party, using at least five interaction phrases.
Support / weaker learners: Use a sentence starter frame with phrases like 'I agree because...' and 'In my opinion...' on their desk.
hw: Record yourself having a 2-minute discussion with a friend about Eid traditions using the interaction phrases.
Write a short story (80-100 words) titled 'My Best Eid Memory', using the past simple and continuous.
Create a list of 10 discussion questions about cultural celebrations to use in next week's class.
tip: For Moroccan learners, explicitly connect the target interaction language to their cultural context of respectful family discussions during Eid, as this makes the task more meaningful and memorable.
